clue.text: The real thing

blocks.note: first meaning: the grammatical name for the word 'the'
second meaning: the genuine article, something that is certainly what it claims

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, 'the real thing', but 'The' is itself the first definition: it is the word grammarians call the definite article.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar names 'the' this way, and colloquially something unmistakably genuine is called this phrase too.

clue.text: EU parliament centre sees new growth for The Greens

blocks.note: the Belgian capital is a seat of the European Parliament
fresh shoots on a plant

explanation.surface: A news report on the Green Party gaining ground in the European Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Greens' looks like the political party; here it is vegetables, the small cabbages served at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: These small cabbage-like buds are leafy vegetables, which cooks call greens.

clue.text: Joining up again after wild gunfire in Yemeni capital

indicators.note: wild suggests something out of control, so the letters run riot into a new order
a capital is the head letter of a word, so only the opening one is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the head of the word Yemeni

explanation.surface: A report of reconciliation in Yemen following a burst of shooting in Sana'a.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a placing instruction but is simply two letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To reunify is to bring divided parts together once more, so reuniting matches joining up again.

clue.text: Lots upset by the Queen's grooms

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so these letters tumble into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: Royal stable hands are distressed by something the monarch has done.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the standard crossword Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostler is a stableman at an inn who looks after guests' horses, which is what a groom does.

clue.text: Legislation rejected by left side of the House?

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word goes the opposite way

blocks.note: a statute or body of rules
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A bill thrown out by the opposition benches in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left side of the House' suggests the political left in the Commons, but 'left' is just L and the definition is a literal side of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: The vertical structures enclosing a building form its sides, so a house's side is one of them.

clue.text: Italian Antonio's out for state ownership

indicators.note: out here means out of order or out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: An Italian called Antonio is campaigning for public control of industry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bringing an industry or company under government control is the process economists call public ownership.

clue.text: Drop stories about places of good interest?

blocks.note: to put down or set down
narratives or reports of events

explanation.surface: An instruction to abandon tales about sightseeing spots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'places of good interest' plays on 'places of interest' for tourists; the interest is what a bank pays on savings.
explanation.definitionFit: Savings held in a bank earn interest, so these accounts are where money gains a good return.

clue.text: Standing alone in empty House of Lords?

blocks.note: first meaning: without equal, unrivalled
second meaning, read literally: a chamber with none of its noble members in it

explanation.surface: A lone member standing in a deserted House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the word: members of the House of Lords are peers, and an empty House has none of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with no equal stands apart, unmatched by any rival in quality.

clue.text: Rouse interest in article on West Africa and Livingstone

blocks.note: the indefinite article
abbreviation
Ken Livingstone, a former Mayor of London

explanation.surface: Stirring curiosity with an article about the explorer David Livingstone in West Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Livingstone suggests the African explorer, but it is the London politician Ken Livingstone, first elected Mayor of London.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir someone's feelings or curiosity, bringing them alive, is to waken them.

clue.text: Old leader slow with Northern Ireland reform

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A former premier dragging his feet on changes in Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Wilson was Labour Prime Minister of Britain in the 1960s and 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Wilson led the British government twice, so he is a past head of state affairs.

clue.text: Money, said father, for sticky sweet

indicators.note: said tells us to go by how the word is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: lolly is British slang for cash
an informal word for dad

explanation.surface: Dad hands over some cash so the child can buy a sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A boiled candy on a stick is sticky to lick, a classic confection for children.

clue.text: Flier needs mark for standard

definitions.note: not a synonym: the word plus 'mark' makes Kitemark, a quality standard

blocks.note: first meaning: a toy flown on a string in the wind
second meaning: add the word mark and you have the British Standards safety symbol

explanation.surface: A pilot must reach a certain grade to qualify.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kitemark is the British Standards Institution's certification symbol stamped on approved products.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper or fabric toy flown on a line soars through the air, and the British quality symbol is named after it.

clue.text: International help, eg for India's redevelopment

indicators.note: redevelopment rebuilds something in a new form, so the letters are reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Development assistance from abroad, such as that sent to rebuild India.
explanation.definitionFit: Money and resources given by one country to another are assistance across national borders.

clue.text: Man overboard in leading boat

blocks.note: surface reading: a sailor has fallen into the sea
setter's reading: the rescue craft that reaches him first is a rubber dinghy blown up with air

explanation.walkthrough: The picture is a sea rescue; the answer names the type of air-filled craft that goes out first to pick up someone from the water.
explanation.definitionFit: Rescue dinghies are often rubber craft filled with air, launched quickly to reach someone fallen from a ship.

clue.text: Brave, perhaps, and embarrassed to hide

blocks.note: flushed with shame
an animal's pelt

explanation.surface: Someone courageous but too ashamed, wanting to go into hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave' is a noun here, an old term for a Native American warrior; the answer is a dated and now offensive word for a Native American.
explanation.definitionFit: A warrior of the indigenous peoples of North America was called a brave in old westerns, an example of the people named.

clue.text: Rotten cargo dump

blocks.note: gone bad, as food does
freight carried by a vehicle

explanation.surface: A shipment of spoiled goods tipped at a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: To get rid of something unwanted by passing it on or unloading it is to dump it.

clue.text: A French king, oddly, has to admit to being nameless

indicators.note: oddly points to the letters in odd-numbered positions, first and third

blocks.note: the French masculine word for a
first and third letters of king
as in own up to, confess

explanation.surface: A French monarch strangely confesses to being anonymous.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone anonymous, whose identity is not known, has no name attached to them.

clue.text: Told to have a good look at political promotional material

indicators.note: told means spoken, so the phrase is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a gander is British slang for a look, and proper means thorough

explanation.surface: Someone is instructed to examine a party's campaign leaflets carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a proper gander' is informal British for 'take a good look'; said in a non-rhotic accent it matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Biased information spread to push a political cause is exactly what campaign leaflets and posters often contain.

clue.text: So the king's not well?

blocks.note: Latin for thus, used to mark a quotation as printed
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king; the 's reads as is

explanation.surface: A question about whether the monarch has fallen ill.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ill or unwell is suffering from disease or nausea.

clue.text: Executive transport docked in France

definitions.note: a place: the answer is a region in France

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so the word loses its end

blocks.note: a chauffeur-driven luxury car for bosses

explanation.surface: A boss's car is parked at a dock somewhere in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' sounds like moored in a harbour, but it means trimmed; the definition is just 'in France', a place there.
explanation.definitionFit: Limousin is a historic region of central France, famed for its cattle and Limoges porcelain.

clue.text: Indignant lover gets sent up

indicators.note: in a down light, sent up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: the Greek god of love

explanation.surface: A partner is cross at being mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent up' looks like mocked, but it signals reversal in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling aggrieved or resentful is being sore, an informal sense chiefly American.

clue.text: Resistance fault repaired without cunning

indicators.note: something repaired is put back together, so these letters are refitted
without in the old sense of outside, so one part goes around the other

blocks.note: R is the physics symbol
taken as written

explanation.surface: An electrical fault in a resistor fixed without any trickery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' seems to mean lacking, but in its old sense it means outside: the rearranged letters wrap around R.
explanation.definitionFit: Being crafty or sly, skilled at deceit, is the sense of both words, as with the Artful Dodger.

clue.text: Harsh critic of one responsible for over-the-top coverage?

blocks.note: first meaning: one who slates, British for criticise severely
second meaning: a roofer, whose work covers the very top of a house

explanation.surface: A scathing reviewer of a journalist who sensationalises the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over-the-top coverage' sounds like hyped reporting, but it is literally the covering on top of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: To slate is British slang for to criticise savagely, and a tradesman laying roof tiles is also so called.

clue.text: Southern trade union sanction on rule backing strikes

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the assembled string runs right to left

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation
approval
a regulation

explanation.surface: A southern union approves a rule supporting industrial action.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers leaving their jobs in protest stage stoppages, which is what industrial strikes are.
